t: A city-state is a city that governs itself and the countryside around it as a state of its own, with its own gods, laws and army and often citizens who share in government.
City-states arose in Sumer, Greece and Phoenicia, among the Maya, on the Swahili coast and in medieval Italy and Germany, usually in clusters of rivals sharing one culture.
Small size encouraged participation, trade and invention but left city-states open to faction and conquest; Singapore, Monaco and Vatican City are their sovereign heirs today.
dyk: Aristotle’s school collected the constitutions of 158 states, but only the Constitution of the Athenians survives, recovered from papyri found in Egypt and first published in 1891.
ev: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grows into the first city and the centre of the earliest known city-state
Eannatum of Lagash records his victory over neighbouring Umma on the Stele of the Vultures
Philip II of Macedon defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea and takes control of mainland Greece
Tikal is defeated by Caracol, an ally of Calakmul, in the wars of the Classic Maya city-states
The Lombard League of Italian communes defeats Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at the Battle of Legnano
The Treaty of Stralsund ends the Hanseatic towns’ war with Denmark at the height of the league’s power
A Portuguese fleet sacks Kilwa and Mombasa, leading city-states of the Swahili coast
Singapore leaves the Federation of Malaysia and becomes an independent city-state

f.power: The citizens or leading families of one city and its farmland, governed by a king, a council, elected magistrates or an assembly under the city’s own laws
f.legitimacy: The city’s gods, founders and laws, and the loyalty of citizens who defended it and shared in its government
f.chosen: Varied: hereditary kings in Sumer and Phoenicia, election or lot among citizens in Greek poleis, councils and elected magistrates in Italian communes and Hanseatic towns
f.examples: Uruk and Lagash (Early Dynastic Sumer), Classical Athens, Carthage, Tikal (Classic Maya), Kilwa Kisiwani (13th–15th centuries), the Republic of Venice
